F16: See the three-entry friction log in the repo: https://github.com/kevin9327/opportunity-radar/blob/main/FRICTION_LOG.md — (1) grants.gov returns two different date formats for the same field across search2 and fetchOpportunity, and the mismatch produced a silent null rather than an error, so a missing deadline shipped as a well-formed answer [HIGH]; (2) an eligibility list that reads only 'Others (see text field entitled Additional Information on Eligibility)' made my tool tell a qualified applicant they were ineligible, which is the difference between a wrong tool and a harmful one [HIGH]; (3) recording the demo with ffmpeg gdigrab captured the desktop and swept in an unrelated window, so I rewrote the recorder to attach to Chrome over CDP and pull frames from the page itself [MEDIUM]. Each entry there has the task, steps, expected vs actual, workaround, and a concrete suggestion.
F15: 1) Documented latency expectations for a spoken turn, and a supported pattern for long-running tools (partial results, or 'working on it' plus a later push). My ranking tool takes ~26s because it runs a local model over several opportunities; that is fine on screen and probably unacceptable out loud, and I had to guess. IMPORTANT. 2) Guidance on writing tool descriptions for voice. My first descriptions were accurate and useless — the router picked plausible-but-wrong tools until I rewrote each one around the question a person asks. On a screen a wrong tool call is visible; on a speaker it is not. IMPORTANT. 3) A machine-readable ISO-8601 date field from grants.gov alongside the display strings, and a boolean for 'eligibility is in prose only'. Both of my HIGH-severity bugs come from consumers having to string-match English. NICE-TO-HAVE for the platform, CRITICAL for anyone building on that API.
F18: MCP (Model Context Protocol, spec 2025-11-25, Streamable HTTP) — implemented the transport by hand in radar/server.py: one endpoint, initialize handing out a session id, optional SSE stream, tools/list schemas generated from Python type hints and docstrings, tools/call returning both spoken text and structuredContent. This is the Alexa+ integration surface. Ollama with Llama 3.1 8B — local fit ranking and utterance routing, so no key or cloud account is needed and the user's query never leaves their machine. grants.gov public API (search2 + fetchOpportunity) — the live data behind all six tools; no key required. Browser Web Speech API — real speech in and out in the Alexa+ simulator (web/). Chrome DevTools Protocol — recording the demo video from inside the page rather than off the desktop. Python standard library only for the server itself; boto3 is an optional dependency for the Bedrock fallback path.
F19: MCP: the spec is precise and small enough to implement in an evening without an SDK, which means the repo has no dependency a judge has to trust. The single-endpoint design with an optional SSE stream suits a self-hosted server — nothing long-lived to babysit, and curl is a working client, which made debugging trivial. Generating tools/list schemas from type hints and docstrings meant the description the model reads is the same text a developer reads, so they cannot drift. Ollama: JSON mode made model output reliably parseable, and the 8B model was good enough to judge relevance and write a one-line reason — it correctly spotted that a solo developer is not eligible for a tribal-organisation grant, a judgement I never hand-coded. grants.gov: public, keyless and generous; counts, close dates, award ceilings and applicant types are all there. Being able to ship a working product with zero credentials is the reason this project exists.
F20: MCP docs: precise about message shape, quiet about what makes a *good* tool description — which mattered more than the transport. A short section on writing tool descriptions for voice would have saved me two hours. Alexa+: I could not find documented latency expectations for a spoken turn, or a supported pattern for a tool that takes 20+ seconds (partial results? push later?). I designed around it with a fast default path, but that was a guess. Ollama: it serialises requests by default — parallelising my calls changed nothing until I found OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL, and setting it as a user environment variable plus restarting the app still did not take effect in my session. For an interactive product that default is a performance cliff you only hit after your architecture assumes otherwise. grants.gov: two date formats for the same field across two endpoints (10/09/2026 vs 'Oct 09, 2026 12:00:00 AM EDT'), which produced a silent null rather than an error; and applicantTypes that sometimes contains only a pointer to prose, which made my eligibility check confidently wrong. Both are in the friction log with suggested fixes.
F21: Excellent, and it is the reason I could finish. MCP: no account, no key, no SDK — read the spec, write a handler, curl it. Zero to a working tools/call in one evening. grants.gov: no signup at all; my first successful query was a single POST with a JSON body, about two minutes from opening the docs. Ollama: one pull command and the model answers on localhost. The common thread is that none of these required me to create an account or enter a card to reach hello world — which matters more than it sounds, because I do not have a card to enter. That constraint is why the ranking layer runs locally, and the local-first design turned out to be the most interesting thing about the project. Alexa+: onboarding was reading rather than installing, since MCP is the integration surface and my server is the thing being onboarded.
F22: Yes, to all of them. MCP: without reservation. Implementing the transport by hand was the right call for a small server, and choosing MCP as the surface meant the same code answers Alexa+ and every other MCP client at once — that is why I could develop against a browser simulator and a local client without a device on my desk. grants.gov: yes; the friction is in the data shape, not the access, and both problems are fixable in a consumer. Ollama: yes, specifically because it keeps the user's question on their machine. The queries people bring to a funding assistant are sentences like 'grants for a family caring for a disabled child', and not having to send that anywhere is a feature, not a compromise. I would want the parallelism default sorted before shipping this to real users. The one thing I would want before building a serious voice product on Alexa+ is documented guidance on slow tools; everything else here I would reach for again tomorrow.
F9: Not submitting for the AWS Builder Mini Challenge, so this is an honest account rather than a claim. Opportunity Radar is deliberately runnable with no cloud account: the data source (grants.gov search2 and fetchOpportunity) is a public keyless API, and fit ranking runs on the user's own machine through Ollama so a sentence describing someone's situation never leaves their house. The code does keep a real Amazon Bedrock path rather than a mention of one: radar/rank.py selects an engine at call time in the order local model -> Bedrock Converse (boto3, converse API, JSON-only judging prompt) -> keyword overlap, and every response reports which engine answered and what it degraded from, so an operator who exports AWS credentials gets Bedrock ranking with no code change. I did not claim the challenge because I could not verify that path against a live account during the hackathon, and claiming an AWS service I had not run would be exactly the kind of unverified answer this project is built to refuse.
F14:
What I did: Opportunity Radar is a new open-source project, published under MIT during the hackathon window and developed entirely in the open. Every commit is on main, including the ones that fixed my own bugs, and the licence is visible at the top of the repository.

How it works: the repo is the whole product, not a demo shell around a hosted service. It contains the MCP server implemented by hand against spec 2025-11-25 over Streamable HTTP (radar/server.py), the six tools with their honesty gates (radar/tools.py), the ranking layer that chooses between a local model, Bedrock and keyword overlap and labels which one answered (radar/rank.py), the utterance router and spoken-answer composer (radar/agent.py), the Alexa+ simulator that shows every MCP call it makes (web/), a 21-test suite (tests/test_radar.py), CI that runs it offline on every push and hits the live source weekly, and the CDP recording pipeline used to produce the demo video (demo/capture.py) so the video itself is reproducible.

Why it matters: anyone can self-host this and point their own Alexa+ at it with no key, no cloud account and no card. The part I hope gets reused is the honesty pattern: the model may set a score and write a reason, but every number, date and URL is attached from the source afterwards, an eligibility list that only points at prose produces 'read the notice' instead of 'you are ineligible', and a dead source produces a refusal instead of an estimate. Those rules are a few dozen lines and the tests that enforce them are shorter still, which makes them easy to lift into any assistant that speaks answers out loud, where a wrong number is invisible.
